doc.title: Ira Gitler interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995

title: Armstrong's sense of form and Decca recordings
summary: Gitler says players kept the chorus they liked, and Armstrong's 1930s Decca records follow a formula of melody, embellishment and climax.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: I want to ask you a thing about him. They say that when Louis Armstrong took a solo it seemingly always had this wonderful finished quality. It wasn’t as if he rambled or was hunting for notes. It’s like when he got to the end it almost had this feeling of almost inevitable correctness.

Well I think a lot of the players then, once they got a certain chorus, remember in-person I don’t know how long they played, but I think I tend to believe that other than at jam sessions, the live performances were a lot like the recordings, you know, just a couple of choruses. Maybe they stretched a little bit more, but I think once they got a chorus they liked, they kind of stayed with that. Now we have alternate takes of things he’s done and they do vary, but they always have certain elements in them, you know I guess something he liked and so I guess he kept it in. And I think he had a great sense of form. But after his period with the Hot Fives and Hot Sevens, when he led his own band or fronted Luis Russell’s band in the thirties made a whole gang of records for Decca, which only recently have begun to be recognized as classics, people dismiss them, you know they’re not that commercial. You know I don’t know what commercial means in that sense, because the tunes may have been pop tunes, but whatever he did with them was transcendent and you find that he had a formula. The first chorus he would play the straight melody, then he would embellish it in the second, then he would, you know, become a little more adventurous in the third chorus and the fourth chorus maybe he’d reach that climactic thing where he ascended into the stratosphere and just made it a grand finish. So it was always, I think he always had a sense of form.
